questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of the kidney?
options: Removal of nitrogenous and acidic wastes
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Production of albumin
questions.suggestedRationale: The liver, not the kidney, produces albumin; the kidney does regulate fluid, excrete wastes, and activate vitamin D.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the normal flow of urine?
options: Collecting duct to the renal pelvis to the ureter to the bladder
Renal pelvis to the urethra to the bladder to the ureter
Ureter to the renal pelvis to the urethra to the bladder
Collecting duct to the ureter to the urethra
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Collecting duct to the renal pelvis to the ureter to the bladder
questions.suggestedRationale: Urine flows from the collecting duct to the renal pelvis, then the ureter, then the bladder (and finally the urethra).

questions.prompt: Which of the following increases glomerular filtration rate?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Increased hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
questions.suggestedRationale: A higher hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries increases GFR; afferent constriction or a higher plasma oncotic pressure would lower it.

questions.prompt: By what process is water reabsorbed from the filtrate?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Osmosis
questions.suggestedRationale: Water is reabsorbed from the filtrate by osmosis, following solute reabsorption.

questions.prompt: Which substance directly controls the reabsorption of water from the collecting ducts?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Antidiuretic hormone
questions.suggestedRationale: ADH (vasopressin) directly controls water reabsorption in the collecting ducts.

questions.prompt: Under what circumstances do cells in the kidneys secrete renin?
options: Blood flow in the afferent arteriole decreases.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Blood flow in the afferent arteriole decreases.
questions.suggestedRationale: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin when afferent arteriolar blood flow or pressure falls (or when NaCl delivery to the macula densa is low).

questions.prompt: Which of the following should be present in the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule and used in co-transport?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Sodium ions
questions.suggestedRationale: Sodium in the filtrate is cotransported with glucose and amino acids in the proximal tubule; cells and plasma proteins should not be in normal filtrate.

questions.prompt: Involuntary urination by a child after age 4 or 5, when bladder control is expected, is referred to as
questions.suggestedLabel: A. enuresis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Enuresis is involuntary urination after the age when bladder control is expected.

questions.prompt: What is the cause of most cases of pyelonephritis?
options: An ascending infection by E. coli
questions.suggestedLabel: A. An ascending infection by E. coli
questions.suggestedRationale: Most pyelonephritis is an ascending infection, most often E. coli from the lower tract.

questions.prompt: Pyelonephritis may be distinguished from cystitis by the presence in pyelonephritis of
options: microbes, leukocytes, and pus in the urine.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. urinary casts and flank pain.
questions.suggestedRationale: Urinary casts and flank pain point to kidney involvement (pyelonephritis); dysuria, urgency, and pyuria also occur in cystitis.

questions.prompt: Which pathophysiological process applies to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Streptococcal infection affects both the glomerular and tubule functions.
Ischemic damage occurs in the tubules, causing obstruction and decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
Immune complexes deposit in glomerular tissue, causing inflammation.
Increased glomerular permeability for unknown reasons
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Immune complexes deposit in glomerular tissue, causing inflammation.
questions.suggestedRationale: Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex (type III) deposition in glomerular tissue.

questions.prompt: What causes the dark urine associated with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Blood and protein leaking through the capillary into the filtrate
Proteinuria and microscopic hematuria from the inflammation
Bleeding from ulcerations in the kidney
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Blood and protein leaking through the capillary into the filtrate
questions.suggestedRationale: Dark “cola” urine comes from red cells and protein leaking through damaged glomeruli into the filtrate.

questions.prompt: Renal disease frequently causes hypertension because
options: congestion and ischemia stimulate release of renin.
damaged tubules absorb large amounts of filtrate
questions.suggestedLabel: B. congestion and ischemia stimulate release of renin.
questions.suggestedRationale: Renal ischemia and congestion stimulate renin release, which raises blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Why does metabolic acidosis develop with bilateral kidney disease?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Tubule exchanges are impaired.
questions.suggestedRationale: Diseased tubules cannot adequately secrete hydrogen ions or regenerate bicarbonate, so metabolic acidosis develops.

questions.prompt: What is the first indicator in the arterial blood gases of acidosis caused by glomerulonephritis?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Decreased bicarbonate ion
questions.suggestedRationale: A falling bicarbonate level is the first typical arterial-blood-gas change of the metabolic acidosis of glomerulonephritis; pH may still be compensated.

questions.prompt: What would be the long-term effects of chronic infection or inflammation of the kidneys?
options: Gradual necrosis, fibrosis, and development of uremia, Kidney failure
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Gradual necrosis, fibrosis, and development of uremia, Kidney failure
questions.suggestedRationale: Chronic infection or inflammation gradually produces necrosis, fibrosis, and eventually uremia and renal failure.

questions.prompt: What factors contribute to headache, anorexia, and lethargy with kidney disease?
questions.suggestedLabel: E. All of the above
questions.suggestedRationale: Hypertension, uremia (elevated urea), anemia, and acidosis can all contribute to headache, anorexia, and lethargy.

questions.prompt: What are the significant signs of nephrotic syndrome?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria
questions.suggestedRationale: Nephrotic syndrome features heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria.

questions.prompt: Common causes of urolithiasis include all of the following EXCEPT
questions.suggestedLabel: B. hyperlipidemia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, and low fluid intake promote stones; hyperlipidemia is not a usual cause of urolithiasis.

questions.prompt: What does hydronephrosis lead to?
options: Ischemia and necrosis in the compressed area
Severe colicky pain radiating into the groin
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Ischemia and necrosis in the compressed area
questions.suggestedRationale: Hydronephrosis compresses renal tissue, leading to ischemia and necrosis if unrelieved.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a predisposing factor to bladder cancer?
options: Exposure to chemicals and cigarette smoke
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Exposure to chemicals and cigarette smoke
questions.suggestedRationale: Bladder cancer is associated with cigarette smoking and occupational chemical exposures (aromatic amines, etc.).

questions.prompt: What is the common initial sign of adenocarcinoma of the kidney?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Microscopic hematuria
questions.suggestedRationale: The usual earliest sign of renal cell (adeno)carcinoma is microscopic hematuria; gross hematuria or pain often comes later.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does NOT usually result from nephrosclerosis?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Acute renal failure
questions.suggestedRationale: Nephrosclerosis leads to ischemia, secondary hypertension, and chronic (not typically acute) renal failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following relates to polycystic kidney disease?
options: It affects only one of the kidneys.
It results in gradual degeneration and chronic renal failure.
The kidneys are displaced and the ureters are twisted.
The prognosis is good because there is adequate reserve for normal life.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. It results in gradual degeneration and chronic renal failure.
questions.suggestedRationale: Adult polycystic kidney disease causes gradual cystic destruction of both kidneys and chronic renal failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a cause for Wilms’ tumor?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. A genetic defect
questions.suggestedRationale: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is associated with genetic defects (for example WT1-related syndromes).

questions.prompt: With severe kidney disease can cause electrolyte imbalance and cause?
options: cardiac arrhythmias and can lead to HF
questions.suggestedLabel: A. cardiac arrhythmias and can lead to HF
questions.suggestedRationale: Severe renal failure causes dangerous electrolyte shifts (especially hyperkalemia) that can trigger arrhythmias and heart failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following indicates the early stage of acute renal failure?
options: Polyuria with urine of fixed and low specific gravity
Very low GFR and increased serum urea
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Very low GFR and increased serum urea
questions.suggestedRationale: The early oliguric phase of acute renal failure shows a very low GFR and a rising serum urea (azotemia).

questions.prompt: What is/are a cause(s) of acute tubule necrosis and acute renal failure?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. All of the above
questions.suggestedRationale: Acute tubular necrosis and acute renal failure can follow prolonged shock, nephrotoxins, or massive crush injury/burns (myoglobinuria).

questions.prompt: Which of the following would likely cause chronic renal failure?
options: Cystitis with pyelonephritis in the right kidney
Obstruction of a ureter by a renal calculus
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Diabetes
questions.suggestedRationale: Diabetes mellitus is a major cause of chronic renal failure; a unilateral stone or a single episode of shock is less typical.

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason for hypocalcemia developing during end-stage renal failure or uremia?
options: Excessive excretion of calcium ions in the urine
A deficit of activated vitamin D and hyperphosphatemia
questions.suggestedLabel: D. A deficit of activated vitamin D and hyperphosphatemia
questions.suggestedRationale: In end-stage renal disease, deficient activated vitamin D and phosphate retention lower serum calcium.

questions.prompt: Cystitis is more common in females because
options: the mucosa in the urinary tract is continuous.
the urethra is short, wide, and adjacent to areas with resident flora.
the pH of urine is more acidic in females.
females have a higher incidence of congenital anomalies
questions.suggestedLabel: B. the urethra is short, wide, and adjacent to areas with resident flora.
questions.suggestedRationale: The female urethra is short and close to perineal flora, which is why cystitis is more common in females.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT likely to lead to hydronephrosis?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Nephrosclerosis
questions.suggestedRationale: Nephrosclerosis is a vascular/ischemic process and does not obstruct urine outflow, so it does not cause hydronephrosis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following congenital defects is a common cause of cystitis in young children?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Vesicoureteral reflux
questions.suggestedRationale: Vesicoureteral reflux lets bladder urine (and bacteria) go back to the kidney and is a common contributor to cystitis/UTI in children.

questions.prompt: Which of the following causes acute renal failure?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Bilateral acute glomerulonephritis
questions.suggestedRationale: Bilateral acute glomerulonephritis can rapidly depress GFR and cause acute renal failure; the other listed conditions are more often chronic or unilateral.

questions.prompt: Uremic signs of renal failure include all of the following EXCEPT
questions.suggestedLabel: B. high blood pressure.
questions.suggestedRationale: Encephalopathy, osteodystrophy, azotemia, and acidosis are uremic features. Hypertension is common in renal failure but is not itself a uremic (waste-product) sign.

questions.prompt: Agenesis is often not diagnosed because
options: the kidney is displaced from its normal position.
it is a genetic defect and asymptomatic until mid-life.
the two functioning kidneys are fused together.
it is usually asymptomatic as one kidney provides adequate function
questions.suggestedLabel: D. it is usually asymptomatic as one kidney provides adequate function
questions.suggestedRationale: Unilateral renal agenesis is often unnoticed because the remaining kidney can provide adequate function.

questions.prompt: Wilms’ tumor is
options: a malignant tumor in the bladder.
an encapsulated mass in one kidney.
not considered to have a genetic origin.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. an encapsulated mass in one kidney.
questions.suggestedRationale: Wilms tumor is typically a large encapsulated malignant mass in one kidney of a young child.

questions.prompt: The micturition reflex is initiated by
options: sympathetic nerves in the sacral spinal cord.
relaxation of the internal sphincter of the bladder.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. increased pressure distending the bladder.
questions.suggestedRationale: Stretch (increased pressure) in the bladder wall initiates the micturition reflex.

questions.prompt: In acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, the glomerular inflammation results from
options: an ascending infection from the bladder.
spread of infection from the tubules
questions.suggestedLabel: B. a type III hypersensitivity reaction.
questions.suggestedRationale: Post-streptococcal glomerular inflammation is a type III immune-complex hypersensitivity, not direct bacterial invasion of the kidney.

questions.prompt: Circulatory shock can affect the kidneys because it causes a decreases in blood pressure which leads to
options: decreased GFR and increased renin secretion.
increased ADH and decreased aldosterone secretion.
sympathetic nervous system (SNS) stimulation and vasodilation of afferent and efferent arterioles.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. decreased GFR and increased renin secretion.
questions.suggestedRationale: A drop in blood pressure reduces GFR and stimulates renin secretion (and can progress to ischemic tubular injury if severe).

questions.prompt: The reabsorption of water and electrolytes by the kidneys is directly controlled by
questions.suggestedRationale: ADH and atrial natriuretic hormone directly adjust water and sodium handling. Angiotensin acts mainly by stimulating aldosterone (more indirect), and bicarbonate level is not a primary controller.

questions.prompt: Uncontrolled essential hypertension may cause chronic renal failure because of
options: predisposition to recurrent urinary tract infections.
damage to afferent arterioles and renal ischemia.
failure of tubules to respond to hormonal controls.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. damage to afferent arterioles and renal ischemia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Long-standing essential hypertension damages afferent arterioles, causing renal ischemia and eventually chronic renal failure.

questions.prompt: Excess urea and other nitrogen wastes in the blood is referred to as
questions.suggestedLabel: B. azotemia.
questions.suggestedRationale: Azotemia is excess urea and other nitrogenous wastes in the blood.

questions.prompt: Urethritis, infection/inflammation of the urethra, is classified into two categories:
questions.suggestedLabel: A. gonococcal and nongonococcal.
questions.suggestedRationale: Urethritis is commonly classified as gonococcal or nongonococcal.
